title: A second engine behind the same door
subtitle: The vendor's executor could not run engines with no key-value cache or an extra output, so a raw-TensorRT backend went in behind the same C interface, and the Rust side never knew

stats.label: copied back to the host per sequence

changed in the vendor's model graph to gather the output to the last token

lede: Hidden-state extraction needs an engine that generates nothing. I built those engines, in Engines for the card you have, and the vendor's executor refused to run them. The runtime has a Rust half that talks to the broker and a C++ half that talks to the GPU, joined by a C interface. So the rule for the second backend was no new configuration surface, no Rust-visible behaviour, and the engine's own tensor enumeration as the only source of truth about what it wants. The C++ library detects the backend kind from the engine's configuration and, for a mining engine, loads it through the raw TensorRT runtime rather than the executor. All of the work happens once, at load.
quote: I did not want the Rust half, the provisioner or the broker to know that mining engines were different.
evidence: TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM engineering: a raw TensorRT backend behind the same C interface for engines with no key-value cache and an extra output, invisible to the Rust side.
Hidden-state extraction: output gathered to the last token by a 6-line graph change, so a batch of 2,000 copies 16 MB to the host instead of 4 GB.
Zero-allocation inference paths: every tensor checked and every buffer allocated once at load, each batch bound in three phases with nothing resolved by name at run time.
Architecture discipline: a first mining path that cloned 13 MB per sequence across 1,600 sequences and copied 300 lines of start-up code was deleted for one path.
author: Corey James
